soil-phys-127.title: Sand boils, where buried water breaks the surface
soil-phys-127.text: In a flood, water pushed through a levee can well up on the dry side as if it were boiling: a sand boil. Turbulent flow at the seep starts soil piping, which can quickly fail the embankment, so crews stack rings of sandbags to slow it. Earthquakes that liquefy saturated sediment make sand boils too, sometimes building a cone called a sand blow. The 1811–1812 New Madrid earthquakes left the largest known, 'The Beach' near Hayti, Missouri, 2.3 kilometres long. Geologists map sand blows as strong evidence of past earthquakes.

soil-phys-070.title: Five sizes of soil pore, from cracks to cryptopores
soil-phys-070.text: A pore's size decides what water it holds and what can live in it. A widely used grouping, after Brewer (1964), sorts soil pores by diameter. The largest class, {{ref:soil-water-189}}, are over 75 μm, too large for significant capillary force. Unless closed off, they drain and are usually full of air at the wetness described in {{ref:soil-water-177}}. They form where soil cracks, where peds and aggregates separate, and along roots and burrows. Mesopores, 30–75 μm, are the largest pores still full of water at that point. Called storage pores, they hold water that plants and soil organisms can use, so soil scientists study them closely for agriculture and irrigation. Micropores, 5–30 μm, hold water that is practically immobile yet still available to plants, so dissolved substances move through them mainly by diffusion. Ultramicropores, 0.1–5 μm, shelter microbes inside aggregates from predators such as amoebae and nematodes, and their volume tracks bacterial biomass. Texture and organic matter set them, and compaction barely touches them. Cryptopores, under 0.1 μm, are too small for most microbes. Organic matter inside them is protected from decay, and their water is barely available to plants.

soil-phys-094.title: Relative density: how close sand is to fully packed
soil-phys-094.text: Relative density measures how densely packed a sand or gravel is. It compares the soil's void ratio in the ground with its maximum and minimum void ratios, which match its very loose and very dense states. A value of 100% means very dense sand or gravel; 0% means extremely loose, unstable soil. It is used for soils whose grains do not stick together, and ASTM D4254-00(2016) sets out how to calculate it.

soil-phys-128.title: Specific storage: water released as pressure falls
soil-phys-128.text: Lower the water pressure in a saturated aquifer and it gives up some of its water. Specific storage is the volume released from a unit volume of aquifer when the hydraulic head, the water's pressure level, falls by one unit. It reflects how compressible both the aquifer and the water are. Storativity, or the storage coefficient, is the same release per unit area of aquifer. For a confined aquifer it is specific storage summed over the thickness. In an unconfined aquifer storativity roughly equals the {{ref:soil-phys-129}}, because release from specific storage is orders of magnitude smaller.

soil-phys-083.title: Compacting soil on purpose to carry a building
soil-phys-083.text: Not all compaction is damage. Builders densify soil on purpose with heavy equipment so it can carry foundations, roads, walkways and retaining structures. Good fill is strong, relatively incompressible, durable, suitably permeable, and stable in volume as its moisture varies. It goes down in layers called lifts. Sands and gravels are usually compacted with vibrating equipment. Silts and clays are often worked with a sheepsfoot roller, whose intense local shearing drives out air. Afterwards, ground to be landscaped must be loosened again so that plants can grow.

soil-phys-089.title: What compaction does to roots, microbes and rivers
soil-phys-089.text: Grassland soil without traffic takes in water five times faster than severely trafficked soil. Compaction chiefly cuts how readily air and water enter the ground. Denser soil with smaller pores restricts roots, partly through build-up of the hormone ethylene, and limits their access to nutrients. Shallow roots can leave the topsoil extremely dry and cracked. Oxygen diffuses poorly, so soil can turn airless. With wetter conditions this boosts {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, raising N2O emissions and leaving less nitrogen for crops. Waterlogged compacted soils also release methane through increased bacterial activity. Severe compaction can shrink microbial biomass and, by removing large pores, shift where earthworms live. Wheel tracks often start runoff and erosion, carrying sediment, nutrients and pesticides off the field to over-enrich lakes and rivers. Less water reaches the groundwater, a serious risk in dry regions. Over large areas, the yield losses may threaten food security.

soil-phys-091.title: Preventing compaction, since cures take decades
soil-phys-091.text: Partly restoring a compacted soil takes several decades, so prevention matters most. Controlled traffic keeps wheel tracks apart from rooting areas, and low tyre pressure spreads a machine's load over a larger surface. Models of field vulnerability help farmers avoid driving on susceptible soil. Where damage is done, deep ripping can loosen compacted layers. Biology helps too. Deep-rooting crops break impermeable layers, add organic matter and drive wetting and drying cycles that crack the soil. Growing crops and trees on the same site, as agroforestry, regenerates compacted soil over the long run. The planting pits described in {{ref:soil-agri-057}}, 20–40 cm across and 10–20 cm deep, are filled with organic matter, capture water and gradually rehabilitate the soil beneath. Adding lime raises pH to suit microbes and earthworms, whose activity loosens the soil. The EU's Seventh Environment Action Programme, in force from 2014, addresses compaction, and a German federal soil law obliges farmers to guard against it.

soil-phys-087.title: How pressure turns loose soil into a dense mass
soil-phys-087.text: Press on soil and it answers by bringing its particles closer. In well-structured soil, particles bond into aggregates, and their stability grows with the number of particle interactions. Applied pressure is met with more particle contacts. The voids shrink, water and air are pushed out, bulk density rises, and water and air pass through less easily. Some soils give way more readily than others. Water films around particles can shield their interactions and weaken structure. So wet soils compact more easily than dry ones, and fine-textured, clay-rich soils more easily than coarse ones. Other traits raise resistance. Angular, mixed structure helps, as does a high starting bulk density. So does organic matter, which binds minerals and water together. Soil pH matters too, because it affects the net charges of molecules.

soil-phys-119.title: Thixotropy: clays that turn liquid when shaken
soil-phys-119.text: Some clays hold firm until disturbed, then flow. Thixotropy is that time-dependent property: a material thick at rest flows more easily when shaken or stressed, then takes time to thicken again. Its particles need time to organise, so many gels and colloids are stable at rest but turn fluid when agitated. Most suspensions of {{ref:soil-chem-100}} behave this way. {{ref:soil-water-071}} switches from stiff solid to liquid mass when disturbed, as slope failures such as the Aberfan disaster show. Herbert Freundlich coined the word, from the Greek for 'touch' and 'turn'.

soil-phys-131.title: Specific weight: density with gravity added
soil-phys-131.text: Water at 4 °C weighs 9.807 kilonewtons per cubic metre. That is its specific weight, or unit weight: weight per unit volume, equal to density multiplied by gravitational acceleration. Unlike density, it is not a fixed property, because gravity varies from place to place. Soil mechanics uses it for earthworks, distinguishing moist, dry and saturated unit weight by whether the pores hold water and air, air only, or water only. Each is calculated from the specific gravity of the solids, the void ratio and the unit weight of water, plus the moisture for moist soil.

soil-phys-067.title: The chemists' pore sizes, measured in nanometres
soil-phys-067.text: To a chemist, a micropore is under 2 nm across. The IUPAC set this standard in 1985: micropores under 2 nm, mesopores of 2 to 50 nm, and a largest class over 50 nm. The limits come from how gases adsorb on rigid solids. Micropores fill cooperatively, mesopores show capillary condensation, and in the largest pores the effects of confinement vanish. The scheme grew out of earlier work by M. M. Dubinin and D. H. Everett. Outside chemistry the limits are often ignored and the prefixes only mark relative sizes, which causes confusion between disciplines.

soil-phys-068.title: Finding the empty space in a sample
soil-phys-068.text: Computed tomography can render the voids inside a sample in three dimensions. Simpler methods also find porosity. Direct methods subtract the volume of the solid skeleton from the bulk volume, and optical ones compare pore and solid areas under a microscope. Water methods weigh a sample soaked and dry, and the difference gives the pore volume. In the gas expansion method, gas passes from the sample's container into an evacuated one, and the ideal gas law gives the answer. It detects only pores open to the surroundings. Mercury intrusion and thermoporosimetry reveal pore sizes.

soil-phys-065.title: Why the most porous soils can drain the slowest
soil-phys-065.text: Clay is full of pores yet gives up water grudgingly. It has very high porosity but very low {{ref:soil-water-193}}: it stores much water per volume but releases it slowly through narrow pore throats. Porosity and ease of flow are only loosely linked. Of two similar sandy aquifers, the more porous one usually conducts water faster, but that rule is inferred rather than direct. Flow tracks the radius of pore throats closely. As grain size or sorting decreases, the tie between throat radius and porosity breaks down, and with it the tie to flow.

soil-phys-064.title: Why heavy clay soils are full of holes
soil-phys-064.text: Sandy soil, typically 1.5 to 1.7 g/cm3 in bulk density, has a porosity between 0.43 and 0.36. Clay soil at 1.1 to 1.3 g/cm3 has between 0.58 and 0.51. Surface porosity falls as particles get coarser, because fine soils build aggregates. Calling clay soils heavy seems to imply few pores; the word reflects their moisture weight and the force needed to pull tools through them. Deeper down, gravity compacts soil, and 0.20 is normal for unsorted gravel-sized material below the biomantle. Traditional models give only approximate results, so fractal, cracking, packed-sphere and other models have been proposed.

soil-phys-066.title: Open, closed, primary and secondary porosity
soil-phys-066.text: Not every pore lets fluid through. Effective, or open, porosity is the fraction where fluid actually flows, excluding closed pores, and it matters for groundwater flow and the movement of dissolved substances. Ineffective, or closed, porosity holds fluids or gases that cannot flow. Pores also differ by origin. Primary porosity is the original pore system of a rock or alluvial deposit. Secondary porosity forms later, as minerals leach out or the rock fractures. Dual porosity treats a medium as two overlapping, interacting reservoirs, such as a rock mass and its fractures.

soil-phys-132.title: Dilatancy: why wet sand dries around a footstep
soil-phys-132.text: On a wet beach, the sand around a walker's foot seems to dry. The foot expands the sand, and water moves into the new space between grains. That is dilatancy, the change in volume of a granular material when it is sheared. In a dense packing, grains interlock and cannot slip past one another, so shearing levers them apart. A very loose material compacts instead. Osborne Reynolds first described it in 1885/1886, and Peter Walter Rowe brought it into geotechnical engineering. The denser the soil, the more it expands, and its friction angle peaks then drops abruptly.

soil-phys-133.title: Pumped dry: how wells make the land sink
soil-phys-133.text: In the United States, the land has sunk 1 m for every 13 m of lost groundwater level. Groundwater-related sinking of land comes from unsustainable pumping. Aquifers often hold compressible silt or clay layers. Pumping changes the effective stress on them, and they consolidate, often irreversibly, lowering the surface. One estimate ties 80% of serious U.S. land sinking to excessive groundwater extraction. The whole San Joaquin Valley has sunk after generations of pumping for crops. Permanent compaction can destroy much of an aquifer's storage, and in Arizona the land kept sinking for decades after water levels recovered by 100 ft.

soil-phys-077.title: Unsaturated soil, where air and water share the pores
soil-phys-077.text: In a saturated aquifer every pore is full of water, so the volume of water equals the porosity. An unsaturated soil holds less water than its porosity, so its pores hold air as well. A moist band just above the saturated zone, where water has climbed by capillarity, divides the two conditions. A whole branch of hydrogeology studies the unsaturated ground. As a soil dries, its connected wet pathways shrink, so its ability to conduct water falls in a strongly non-linear way. Water moving into dry soil often advances in fingers, because the boundary between wet and dry zones is unstable.

soil-phys-099.title: Matric suction, the pull that holds damp soil together
soil-phys-099.text: Above the groundwater, soil water is under tension rather than pressure. Matric suction is that negative pore water pressure in unsaturated soil, caused by surface tension in the pores and defined as pore air pressure minus pore water pressure. Because the water pressure is negative, effective stress there is slightly greater than total stress. Capillary rise is inversely proportional to pore diameter, so sandy soils have much shallower capillary zones than clays and silts. Heavy rain soaking in lowers the suction, cutting the soil's shear strength and the stability of slopes. It is measured with the instrument described in {{ref:soil-water-221}}.

soil-phys-061.title: Measuring bulk density with a metal core and an oven
soil-phys-061.text: A metal corer is driven into the soil at a chosen depth and horizon, cutting out a sample of known volume. Weighed moist, the core gives the wet, or total, bulk density. Then it goes into an oven, often at 105 °C until its weight stops changing, leaving the mass of solids. The weight lost on drying is mostly water. Dry bulk density is the oven-dry mass divided by the total volume; wet bulk density counts the liquids too.
